documents.unit: UGA Leadership Council on AI / Provost
documents.title: UGA Guidance on Acceptable Use of AI (companion to Policy 01.07.005)
documents.stance_why: The preamble says "The UGA community is encouraged to explore these important tools and to use them responsibly", then attaches conditions: use "must (i) align with the University's mission" and "(ii) comply with applicable federal and state laws". This is permission with conditions, not delegation, because the document itself sets the terms, so permit.
documents.summary: The guidance is a university-wide acceptable-use document tied to Policy 01.07.005 covering data privacy, vetted tools, accountability and examples of AI use across teaching, research and operations. It welcomes responsible AI use and sets conditions (law, data protection, verification), but gives no rule for student coursework.

units.why: The preamble says "The UGA community is encouraged to explore these important tools and to use them responsibly", a welcoming default for everyone, so P02 (permit or encourage by default), actor all, general phase.
units.anchor: The UGA community is encouraged to explore these important tools and to use them responsibly

units.why: "their use must (i) align with the University's mission and values ... and (ii) comply with applicable federal and state laws" sets a binding condition on all AI use, which is a compliance rule, so P77 rather than P56.
units.anchor: their use must (i) align with the University's mission and values
units.fit_note: Also requires alignment with the University's mission and values for integrity and fairness, which P77 does not name.

units.why: "This guidance aims to mitigate AI-related risks such as misuse, abuse, inappropriate repurposing" states the purpose and scope of the guidance, so it is the institution-wide framework type P56.
units.anchor: This guidance aims to mitigate AI-
units.policy: The guidance aims to mitigate AI-related risks such as misuse, abuse, inappropriate repurposing, and misalignment between systems and users.

units.why: "the policy will control" says which text wins if the guidance and Policy 01.07.005 differ. It is a framework statement about how the guidance relates to the policy, so P56, with a note because P80 (who interprets) does not fit.
units.anchor: For any inconsistencies between this guidance and the policy, the policy will control.
units.fit_note: Sets precedence of Policy 01.07.005 over this guidance, which P56 does not name.

units.why: "Approved by the UGA Leadership Council on AI on February 21, 2025 / Approved by the Provost on March 5, 2025" says by which body and when the guidance was adopted, so P84.
units.anchor: Approved by the UGA Leadership Council on AI on February 21, 2025

units.why: The revision note says "Section 2g ... was updated to align with the policy ... by revision effective August 7, 2026", recording that the guidance is revised over time, so P54 (revisit regularly) fits as nearest type.
units.anchor: revision effective August 7, 2026
units.fit_note: Records an actual revision rather than a commitment to future review.

units.why: The definition "the term 'AI' as used herein encompasses Generative AI (GAI)" sets what the guidance covers, so P61 (define AI and scope).
units.anchor: The term 'AI' as used herein encompasses Generative AI (GAI).

units.why: "the term 'data' is defined broadly and includes any text, documents, images, video, etc. that a user includes in AI models" defines the data the privacy rules cover, so P61 (scope definition) rather than P50 because it states no duty.
units.anchor: includes any text, documents, images, video, etc. that a user includes in AI

units.why: "Users of AI should adhere to applicable international, foreign, federal, and state laws and regulations, as well as USG and UGA data policies" tells users to follow existing law and policy, so P77.
units.anchor: Users of AI should adhere to applicable international, foreign, federal, and state laws

units.why: "Permission to access UGA data does not constitute permission to use that data in AI models" bars putting UGA data into AI tools merely because one can access it, a data-protection rule, so P50.
units.anchor: Permission to access UGA data does not constitute permission to use that data in AI
units.frag_end: begin by discussing it with their supervisor.
units.fit_note: Frames data protection as a permission rule for employees rather than advice about tool storage.

units.why: "The user is responsible for seeking permission and guidance in using UGA data in novel ways such as in an AI tool and should begin by discussing it with their supervisor" tells the person to ask before an uncertain AI use, so P10, noting it is about employees and supervisors.
units.anchor: should begin by discussing it with their supervisor
units.fit_note: Directs employees to ask a supervisor, not students to ask an instructor.

units.why: "AI users should adhere to ethical standards and safeguard the rights and privacy of human participants" with a pointer to the Human Research Protection Program governs AI in human-subjects research, so P62.
units.anchor: safeguard the rights and privacy of human participants when using human-related data

units.why: "All data used in AI projects must be handled in compliance with the University's data privacy policies" is a data-privacy duty, so P50.
units.anchor: All data used in AI projects must be handled in compliance with the University's data

units.why: "The user is expected to determine whether privacy impact assessments must be conducted by UGA" calls for institutional privacy review of AI projects, nearest to P65 (review of AI tools and data sharing).
units.anchor: determine whether privacy impact assessments must be conducted by UGA
units.fit_note: The review is a privacy impact assessment of a project, not approval of a tool or vendor.

units.why: "Users of AI should take care when using personally identifiable information in AI tools" is a personal-data protection rule, so P50.
units.anchor: Users of AI should take care when using personally identi

units.why: "If AI is used to inform decision-making, the user should outline for recipients of that decision how AI was used" is a disclosure duty about AI in decisions, so P24 (disclose AI use), noting the context is institutional decisions.
units.anchor: the user should outline for recipients of that decision how AI was used in the
units.fit_note: Disclosure is to recipients of a university decision, not with a student submission.

units.why: "AI should not take the place of human-centered approaches to decision-making, nor should AI be used in automated decision-making with regard to university processes" keeps humans in charge of decisions, so P73.
units.anchor: nor should AI be used in automated decision-making with regard to university processes

units.why: "Users that generate content through AI ... should clearly indicate the use of AI in the creation of the content" requires labeling AI-made content, so P24 (disclosure), applying to websites and brochures rather than coursework.
units.anchor: should clearly indicate the use of AI in the creation of the content
units.fit_note: Covers university communications content (websites, brochures), not student submissions.

units.why: "should only use AI tools that have been properly acquired through the Procurement process, which includes vetting by EITS" for sensitive data tells users to use vetted tools, so P92.
units.anchor: should only use AI tools that have been properly acquired through the Procurement process
units.frag_end: compliance with state and federal laws (e.g., FERPA).
units.fit_note: The limit applies when working on sensitive or restricted data.

units.why: "Users who wish to use new AI tools ... that are not already vetted by EITS should begin by discussing it with their supervisor" asks users to consult before using an unvetted tool, so P10 with a note.
units.anchor: that are not already vetted by EITS should begin by discussing it with their supervisor
units.fit_note: Ask-first applies to unvetted tools and a supervisor, not to course use.

units.why: "must ensure that the models install fully locally and the associated tools do not link to any digital infrastructure on the Cloud" is a specific condition for free or open-source models on sensitive data that no existing type captures.
units.anchor: must ensure that the models install fully locally
units.uncovered_note: For sensitive or restricted data, only fully local, unmodified open-weight models from trusted sources may be used.

units.why: "AI can be used to support educational activities, such as providing personalized learning experiences, offering tutoring assistance, and enhancing accessibility" names benefits of AI for teaching and learning without a rule, so P87.
units.anchor: providing personalized learning experiences, offering tutoring assistance, and enhancing accessibility for students

units.why: "AI technologies can be employed to streamline administrative tasks, such as scheduling, resource allocation, and data management" lists acceptable operational uses, so P76.
units.anchor: AI technologies can be employed to streamline administrative tasks

units.why: "AI can be used to support research activities, including data analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling" permits AI for data analysis, so P89.
units.anchor: AI can be used to support research activities, including data analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive

units.why: "researchers should review the separate AI guidance from the UGA Office of Research" defers research use to another office, which is P62 (defer to other rules for research).
units.anchor: researchers should review the separate AI guidance from the UGA Office of Research

units.why: "AI can assist in providing student services, such as career counseling, general wellness resources, and academic advising" permits AI in student services, so P76 (operational use).
units.anchor: AI can assist in providing student services, such as career counseling, general wellness resources, and

units.why: "carefully avoiding the handling of sensitive or restricted data, such as health-related information" limits what student-service chatbots may handle, a data-protection rule, so P50.
units.anchor: carefully avoiding the handling of sensitive or restricted data

units.why: "Regardless of the tools employed, individuals are responsible for the integrity and accuracy of their work" makes people accountable for what they produce with AI, so P29.
units.anchor: Regardless of the tools employed, individuals are responsible for the integrity and accuracy of their

units.why: "This includes verifying the accuracy of information generated by AI and ensuring it is free from errors and biases" tells users to check AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: verifying the accuracy of information generated by AI and ensuring it is free from errors

units.why: "It is essential to exercise caution to avoid copyright infringement when using GAI tools. Users must respect intellectual property rights" concerns copyright of AI output, so P52.
units.anchor: exercise caution to avoid copyright infringement when using GAI tools

documents.title: Academic Honesty & Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page says "the default rule for student use of AI on their coursework is that it is not permitted unless it is explicitly authorized by the course instructor", which is a ban unless permitted. It also lets each instructor decide, but the stated default is the document's own position, so restrict rather than delegates.
documents.summary: The CTL page states UGA's default that student AI use is not permitted unless the course instructor authorizes it, and leaves acceptable use to each instructor. Most of the page explains how to use and interpret Turnitin's AI Writing Detector with caution, and when to report to the Office of Academic Honesty.

units.why: "the default rule for student use of AI on their coursework is that it is not permitted unless it is explicitly authorized by the course instructor" states what applies when nothing is authorized, so P06 (fallback rule); P01 is a flat ban, which this is not.
units.anchor: it is not permitted unless it is explicitly authorized by the course instructor

units.why: "the instructor of record can determine what constitutes acceptable use of GAI by students" puts the decision with each instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: the instructor of record can determine what constitutes acceptable use of GAI by students

units.why: "it is important to proactively engage students in an open discussion about your expectations regarding GAI" tells instructors to talk with students about the rules, so P66.
units.anchor: proactively engage students in an open discussion about your expectations regarding GAI

units.why: "is the use of GAI off-limits, sometimes OK, or always encouraged?" lists the range of positions an instructor may take, a simple set of categories, so P05 with a note that it is only an example.
units.anchor: is the use of GAI off-limits, sometimes OK, or always encouraged?
units.fit_note: Gives three example positions, not formally named tiers.

units.why: "Turnitin's AI Writing Detector is the only AI Writing Detector approved for use at UGA" names the approved detector, so P40 (detection tools used), with a note that it is an approval rule.
units.anchor: Turnitin's AI Writing Detector is the only AI Writing Detector approved for use at UGA
units.fit_note: States which detector is approved rather than requiring detection.

units.why: "UGA instructors should not use AI detectors that are not supported by UGA, as these other tools have not been vetted ... for FERPA compliance" bars unvetted tools for privacy reasons, so P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: UGA instructors should not use AI detectors that are not supported by UGA

units.why: "scores between 1% and 19% are replaced by an asterisk to indicate that the score is less reliable" and a "higher incidence of false positives" between 1-20% describe the detector's unreliability, so P39.
units.anchor: there is a higher incidence of false positives when the score is between 1-20%
units.fit_note: Describes partial unreliability and how the tool handles low scores.

units.why: "It is important that Turnitin scores not be used as a definitive measure of misconduct" sets a limit on detector evidence, so P69.
units.anchor: Turnitin scores not be used as a definitive measure of misconduct

units.why: "carefully analyze the work and compare it to past student writing" tells instructors what other evidence to weigh when AI use is suspected, so P69.
units.anchor: carefully analyze the work and compare it to past student writing

units.why: "instructors have a responsibility to report to the Office of Academic Honesty" is a required reporting step once a violation is believed, so P81.
units.anchor: instructors have a responsibility to report to the Office of Academic Honesty

units.why: "A facilitated discussion will be scheduled for you to talk with the student about their process for completing the assignment" has the instructor talk with the student about the work, so P57, with a note that the Office schedules it.
units.anchor: A facilitated discussion will be scheduled for you to talk with the student about their
units.fit_note: The talk is facilitated by the Office of Academic Honesty after a report, not before escalating.

units.why: "instructors should use Turnitin's AI Writing Detector with caution" says not to trust detector results fully, so P39.
units.anchor: instructors should use Turnitin's AI Writing Detector with caution

units.why: "sentence-level false positive rate of 4%, but studies show that this false positive rate is higher for students who speak English as a second language" explains why the detector is unreliable, so P39, with a note on the equity concern.
units.anchor: this false positive rate is higher for students who speak English as a second language
units.fit_note: Also names a bias against second-language writers, which P39 does not.

units.why: "it is not possible for any AI detection tool to offer such context or suspected source" says detector flags cannot be checked against a source, so P39.
units.anchor: it is not possible for any AI detection tool to offer such context or suspected

units.why: "Those with the resources to access more sophisticated tools than GPT-3.5 are better able to avoid detection" says detectors lag behind new models, so P39.
units.anchor: Those with the resources to access more sophisticated tools than GPT-3.5 are better able to
units.fit_note: Adds that detection gaps favor students with more resources.

documents.title: Generative AI Policies for Teaching & Learning
documents.stance_why: The resource sets no rule of its own: it says "start with your learning goals and work backward" and offers an "AI Assessment Scale" with "five 'levels'", a "traffic light" chart, and sample policies "representing varying stances ... (highly permissive, moderately permissive, or maximally restrictive)". Because it offers tiers and templates for instructors to choose from, stance is delegates and the tiers are listed.
tiers: AI Assessment Scale: No AI / AI Planning / AI Collaboration / Full AI / AI Exploration
Sample syllabus policies: highly permissive / moderately permissive-mixed / maximally restrictive
documents.summary: The CTL resource helps instructors design AI rules for their own courses. It offers the five-level AI Assessment Scale, a traffic-light chart, declaration and reflection templates, and three sample syllabus policies ranging from permissive to prohibitive.

units.why: "course policies should include ... Explicit statement of the rule, with the boundaries clearly explained" asks instructors to state the AI rule in the course policy, so P09.
units.anchor: Explicit statement of the rule, with the boundaries clearly explained.

units.why: "Brief explanation of the rationale for the rule" asks instructors to give students their reasons, so P66.
units.anchor: Brief explanation of the rationale for the rule.

units.why: "Use of personal pronouns ... to help personalize the policies and begin to establish a sense of personal responsibility" advises on how to word the rules, so P66 (word the rules with care).
units.anchor: Use of personal pronouns

units.why: "start with your learning goals and work backward from there" ties the decision on AI to learning objectives, so P83.
units.anchor: start with your learning goals and work backward from there

units.why: "Which tasks represent critical learning moments, where productive struggle ... will benefit students" asks the instructor to decide which tasks need unaided work, linking the AI rule to learning objectives, so P83 (P41 would fit if it said AI shortcuts practice).
units.anchor: critical learning moments

units.why: "Which tasks are necessary but not central to your learning goals (e.g., proofreading, formatting)? Could use of generative AI tools ... free your students up" suggests allowing AI on peripheral tasks, so P91 (editing and proofreading help), phrased as a question to instructors.
units.anchor: necessary but not central to your learning goals
units.fit_note: Also frames the choice as freeing students to focus on deeper thinking.

units.why: "Which tasks are new to students, and with which do they already have experience?" tells instructors to consider student experience when setting the rule, so P83 with a note (it echoes P42, but gives no rule for novices).
units.anchor: new to students
units.fit_note: Student experience, not only learning objectives, is a factor.

units.why: "The AI Assessment Scale identifies five 'levels' of generative AI use" and lists them, so P05 (named tiers).
units.anchor: The AI Assessment Scale identifies five 'levels' of generative AI use

units.why: "No AI (Assessment completed without assistance and in a controlled environment...)" is the scale level with no AI in a controlled setting, so P22, with a note that it is one level of a scale.
units.anchor: Assessment completed without assistance and in a controlled environment
units.fit_note: Defined as one level of an assessment scale rather than as an exam rule.

units.why: "AI Planning (Assessment emphasizes ability to independently develop and refine ideas ... brainstorming, outlining, initial research)" lets AI help with planning and ideation, so P15.
units.anchor: AI Planning

units.why: "AI Collaboration (Generative AI may be used to help complete the task, while students critically evaluate and modify the AI-generated outputs.)" allows AI help with checking, so P16 as nearest, with a note.
units.anchor: Generative AI may be used to help complete the task, while students critically evaluate and
units.fit_note: Allows AI help on the task with critical evaluation, not stated limits on size or citation.

units.why: "Full AI (Generative AI may be used to complete any elements of the task, and possibly being required for the assessment.)" is the level where AI is open or required, so P79.
units.anchor: Generative AI may be used to complete any elements of the task
units.fit_note: Describes AI as open to any element and possibly required.

units.why: "AI Exploration (Generative AI used creatively to enhance problem-solving, generate novel insights, or develop innovative solutions)" is a scale level that encourages creative AI use, so P15.
units.anchor: Generative AI used creatively to enhance problem-solving, generate novel insights
units.fit_note: Covers creative and problem-solving use, wider than brainstorming.

units.why: "you may also find it helpful to require students to include statements declaring/ citing their use of generative AI" suggests requiring a statement with each submission, so P24.
units.anchor: require students to include statements declaring/ citing their use of generative AI

units.why: "Practices around the citation and declaration of the use of generative AI are still evolving" admits that the rules will change, so P54, with a note that it refers to disclosure practice.
units.anchor: Practices around the citation and declaration of the use of generative AI are still evolving
units.fit_note: Says disclosure practice is still changing, not that the CTL guidance will be revised.

units.why: "For citation guidelines, it is best to consult the style guides associated with your chosen citation style" sends instructors to style guides for citing AI, so P24.
units.anchor: it is best to consult the style guides associated with your chosen citation style
units.fit_note: Defers the citation format to external style guides.

units.why: "ask students to include a statement with their assignment that provides a 'declaration' of their use (or lack thereof)" recommends a declaration with each submission and says it holds students "accountable", so P24.
units.anchor: ask students to include a statement with their assignment that provides a 'declaration' of their

units.why: "requiring a declaration from students may also increase your own workload ... Taking stock of this tradeoff is an important calculus" warns instructors about grading burden, which no type names, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: requiring a declaration from students may also increase your own workload
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should weigh the extra grading workload against the benefit of requiring AI declarations.

units.why: "Which specific generative AI tools were used ... What prompts did you input ... How did you incorporate the output" lists the details a declaration should give, so P25.
units.anchor: What prompts did you input into the generative AI tools?

units.why: "I take responsibility for the contents of my submitted work" in a sample statement has the student own what they submit after reviewing AI output, so P29.
units.anchor: I take responsibility for the contents of my submitted work.

units.why: "Asking students to reflect on their use of generative AI ... building personal responsibility, applying critical thinking, and increasing their AI literacy" recommends a reflection on AI use, so P26.
units.anchor: Asking students to reflect on their use of generative AI for their work serves several
units.frag_end: approaching the use of generative AI for their work.

units.why: "Sample syllabus policy" Example 1 says "thoughtful and creative engagement with AI is encouraged. Therefore, you will not be penalized", a permit-by-default policy, so P02.
units.anchor: thoughtful and creative engagement with AI is encouraged

units.why: "AI tools are best used to augment, not replace, our skills" keeps AI in a supporting role, so P32.
units.anchor: AI tools are best used to augment, not replace, our skills

units.why: "You are responsible for assessing the validity and applicability of any GAI output incorporated into your work" requires students to check AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: You are responsible for assessing the validity and applicability of any GAI output

units.why: "If you provide minimum effort prompts, you will receive low quality results. Practice careful prompt engineering." advises on writing prompts, so P93.

units.anchor: Refrain from entering information of a highly personal or

units.anchor: For Generative AI, that may include prompts, specific AI used, and date.

units.why: "The use of Generative AI (GAI) tools is not generally permitted in this course, but will be permitted for select assignments" makes AI banned by default with named exceptions, so P08 does not fit (no staging by skill); P04 fits because each assignment sets the rule.
units.anchor: is not generally permitted in this course, but will be permitted for select assignments
units.fit_note: Default is no AI, with permission per assignment.

units.why: "Specific assignments will include details about whether use of GAI tools is allowable or not, and why" says the assignment instructions give the rule and reasons, so P09.

units.anchor: you may not represent output generated by a GAI tool as your own work

units.why: "Any such use of GAI output must be appropriately cited or disclosed, including quotation marks and in-line citations for direct quotes" requires disclosure of AI use, so P24.
units.anchor: must be appropriately cited or disclosed, including quotation marks and in-line citations for direct quotes

units.why: "Including anything you did not write in your assignment without proper citation will be treated as an academic misconduct case" classifies undisclosed use as misconduct, so P36; it also makes nondisclosure the violation, which P28 covers, but P36 is the main point.
units.anchor: will be treated as an academic misconduct case

units.why: "Suspected unauthorized assistance, plagiarism, or other violations ... will be reported to the Office of Academic Honesty" is a required report step, so P81.
units.anchor: will be reported to the Office of Academic Honesty

units.why: "I recommend that you do not have your assignment and the GAI tool open on your device at the same time" keeps the AI and the work apart, so P23.

units.why: "the use of generative AI (GAI) tools is strictly prohibited. This includes all stages of your work process, even the preliminary ones." bans AI on all work, so P01.
units.anchor: the use of generative AI (GAI) tools is strictly prohibited

units.why: "To ensure you develop and master the foundational knowledge and skills in this course" gives the reason for the ban, protecting foundations, so P42.
units.anchor: To ensure you develop and master the foundational knowledge and skills in this course

units.why: "This prohibition extends to AI writing tools like Grammarly and Wordtune, as well as GAI tools like ChatGPT, Copilot" names the tools covered by the ban, so P18, noting it is about prose tools.
units.anchor: This prohibition extends to AI writing tools like Grammarly and Wordtune

units.why: "If you are uncertain about using a particular tool to support your work, please consult with me before using it." in the restrictive sample asks students to ask first, so P10.
